Subject: Contingency buffer for Dedicated GPU pool — options

Hi Elaine,

Thanks again for taking the time today. As discussed, SyncByte's traffic has a strong diurnal pattern plus unpredictable spikes from batch jobs — you asked about ways to avoid throttling while not overcommitting up front. I sketched two pragmatic options for the Dedicated GPU pool that should preserve throughput SLOs without locking you into a large permanent uplift: 

Option A — Contingency buffer (reserved buffer add-on)
- Add a 10% reserved buffer on top of your current pool (billed as reserved capacity).
- Pricing: +15% on top of your current committed rate (annualized), with normal reserved discount tiers applying.
- Throughput guarantee: buffer is backed by our reserved pool routing and will not be preempted.
- Upside: predictable performance for burst windows.
- Downside: committed cost increases immediately.

Option B — Burst buffer + temporary conversion policy
- Add a non-committed burst pool (soft capacity) sized ~10% that is billed at a blended "burst" rate (pooled metered rate, no fixed commit).
- If sustained usage > commit + burst for > 72 hours, we offer an automatic temporary conversion to committed capacity (prorated) or a one-time usage credit if they decline conversion.
- Upside: no long-term spend increase unless used; more flexible.
- Downside: slightly higher per-unit price for burst usage.

Trade-offs and proposed concession (we can be flexible):
- If SyncByte signs a 6-month amendment to lock the new pool level (commit+10% buffer), Redwood can offer a one-month credit applied to the first billing cycle of the amendment.
- If you prefer Option B, we can cap the effective burst rate to limit surprise invoices and include a 7-day prior-notification for conversion.

I'm attaching a simple workbook that models cost/usage scenarios (contingency_pricing_workbook.xlsx). If you want, I can run our throughput simulator on a sample of your 7-day traces to estimate hit rates and expected cost delta.

Next step: tell me whether SyncByte prefers the reserved buffer (A) or the burst model (B) and whether procurement needs a redline of the amendment. Happy to get this into DocuSign once we align.

Best,
Avery

Avery / Marissa — quick commercial take:

1) How buffer counts toward committed minimums
- Option A (reserved buffer): counts fully toward the committed minimum for the amendment period. That's straightforward and aligns with our billing system.
- Option B (burst): does NOT count toward committed minimums — it's metered. However, if customer requests conversion, we can do a prorated conversion with an effective start date at conversion (pro-rated invoice for the calendar month).

2) Blended burst rate
- Recommend billing burst at 1.35x the effective per-unit committed rate (this preserves our margin while giving them a meaningful savings vs on-demand GPUs).
- Alternatively, if we want a softer approach, 1.2x with a 5% buffering credit if they agree to a 6-month roll-up.

3) One-month credit mechanics
- Offer as an invoice credit (applied to the first invoice of the amendment). It's clean from accounting and easier for procurement acceptance. Note: invoice credits require finance sign-off but we do this often for mid-term lock-ins.

4) Auto-conversion vs manual
- Recommend manual conversion by default (customer confirmation required). If they insist on auto, require 72-hour notification and allow a one-time opt-out credit equal to 33% of the converted period's monthly charge. Auto conversion creates operational and AR complexity; avoid unless customer signs a strict SLA.

I'll attach a short workbook with modeled scenarios showing expected delta under mild, medium, and heavy spike patterns (contingency_pricing_workbook.xlsx).

If you want me to sign off on a redline for the amendment, I can draft language for: commit accounting, burst billing rate, manual conversion workflow, invoice-credit mechanics, and a one-month welcome credit.

— Karthik
Director, Sales Strategy | Redwood Inference
